title: Moving from RISC-V to Arm
summary: Translate a function’s register roles and width, then run its Arm version in the other lab.

sections.heading: What carries over
prose: Your knowledge of bits, memory, control flow and functions still applies. This guide compares RV64 with Arm A64. Check the calling convention, result width and execution environment as you translate.
A calling convention is the agreement between a function and its caller. The table shows ordinary integer-register roles used by the worked function.

sections.heading: Check the register names
prose: Arm `x0` is an ordinary register used for the first argument and result. It does not have the always-zero meaning of RISC-V `x0`.

In Arm, `w0` names the low 32 bits of the same 64-bit register named `x0`. A write through a `w` name clears the upper half of its `x` register. RV64 W arithmetic copies result bit 31 into the upper half. Keep the worked function 64 bits wide in both versions.

The preserved general-purpose integer registers differ: RISC-V uses `s0`–`s11`; Arm uses `x19`–`x29`. Restore `sp` to its incoming value before returning, and keep it 16-byte aligned. A function that makes a nested call must protect its incoming return address and values needed afterwards.

sections.heading: Translate a difference function
prose: Both functions return the low 64 bits of `now - then`. Their caller supplies `now` first and `then` second. The destination is also the first input, so the subtraction replaces `now` with the difference. Neither function makes a further call.
These are function bodies, with no process startup or reporting code. The Arm source is read-only in this RISC-V lab; use the linked Arm exercise to run Arm instructions.

snippets.label: RISC-V RV64 function
snippets.source:
difference:
  sub a0, a0, a1
  ret

snippets.label: Arm A64 function, read-only here
snippets.source:
difference:
  sub x0, x0, x1
  ret

sections.heading: Know what the lab supplies
prose: Here, GNU tools assemble and link your source. A CPU emulator runs the executable as an xv6 user process. For fragments, the lab supplies entry, stack setup, register capture, reporting and exit. Tools → Program shows that complete program.

The core Arm lessons run supported functions in a browser simulator. The lesson supplies arguments and recognises the function’s return. That course’s GNU/QEMU and physical-board activities have their own startup and debugging instructions.

A function body returns to its caller. A top-level fragment continues into the supplied capture code. A complete program supplies its own entry and exit. System calls, valid addresses and device access depend on the environment; xv6 system calls differ from Linux’s.

sections.heading: Run the RISC-V caller
prose: Copy the caller and function below. Then open the RISC-V playground to run the function independently. Choose Tools → Projects → New project. Select Assembly fragment, give it a name and choose Create project. Paste the copied code into the editor.

snippets.label: RISC-V assembly fragment with a caller
snippets.source:
li a0, 53
li a1, 40
call difference
mv t2, a0
j done
difference:
  sub a0, a0, a1
  ret
done:

after: Choose Build & Run, then find `t2` in Registers. Compare it with the difference of the two loaded arguments. The call enters `difference`. After `ret` returns, `mv t2, a0` copies the result into the default result display. Then `j done` skips the function body before the lab captures registers.

Start stepping runs the supplied entry and setup, then pauses before the first machine instruction in your fragment. Step instruction advances through the executed instructions; a source line may expand into several. Tools → Program shows the supplied program and its machine instructions.

sections.heading: Try a fresh Arm function
prose: Open the Arm transfer appendix and find Translate an adjusted difference. Its editor supplies 64-bit now, then and adjustment values in `x0`, `x1` and `x2`. Write the low-64-bit result of now minus then plus adjustment into `x0`, keeping `x1` and `x2` unchanged. Choose Run tests and inspect the fresh calls, including inputs wider than 32 bits.

The same page shows the Arm calling convention before the task. Identify which RISC-V registers would carry those three arguments. Explain why using a `w` destination could change the function’s result.

sections.heading: Compare flags and branches below
prose: The runnable RISC-V example below checks carry explicitly. Arm flag-setting arithmetic records NZCV; ordinary `add` and `sub` preserve it. RISC-V integer arithmetic has no NZCV flags. Its branches compare registers directly. Use the example and optional exercise to check the required unsigned relationship.
